'''Jonathon Noë Joseph Pines''' (born 11 October 1961<ref name=whoswho/>) is head of the Cancer Biology Division at the [[Institute of Cancer Research]] in London. He was formerly a senior group leader at the [[Gurdon Institute]] at the [[University of Cambridge]].<ref name=fmedsci>{{cite web|author=Anon|year=2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160510153409/http://www.acmedsci.ac.uk/fellows/fellows-directory/ordinary-fellows/dr-jonathon-pines/|archive-date=2016-05-10|url=http://www.acmedsci.ac.uk/fellows/fellows-directory/ordinary-fellows/dr-jonathon-pines/|publisher=acmedsci.ac.uk|location=London|title=Dr Jonathon Pines FMedSci}}</ref><ref name=gurdon>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160309030608/http://www.gurdon.cam.ac.uk/research/pines|archive-date=2016-03-09|url=http://www.gurdon.cam.ac.uk/research/pines|publisher=University of Cambridge|location=Cambridge|title=Jonathon Pines PhD FMedSci, Cancer Research UK Director of Research in Cell Division, Member of the Zoology Department}}</ref>

==Education==
Pines was educated at the [[University of Cambridge]] where he was awarded a PhD in 1987 for research on cyclin in [[sea urchin]] eggs<ref>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=University of Cambridge|title=Cyclin: a major maternal message in sea urchin eggs|first= Jonathon Noe Joseph|last=Pines|year=1987|url=https://idiscover.lib.cam.ac.uk/permalink/f/t9gok8/44CAM_ALMA21431191210003606|website=cam.ac.uk|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.233321}}|oclc=499166627}}</ref> supervised by [[Tim Hunt]].<ref name=timhunt>{{cite journal |last1=Pines |first1=Jonathon |last2=Hunt |first2=Tim |year=1987 |title=Molecular cloning and characterization of the mRNA for cyclin from sea urchin eggs |journal=[[The EMBO Journal]] |volume=6 |issue=10 |pages=2987–2995|pmid=2826125|pmc=553735 |doi=10.1002/j.1460-2075.1987.tb02604.x}}</ref><ref name=zoo/>

==Research and career==
Following his PhD, Pines was a [[postdoctoral researcher]] supervised by [[Anthony R. Hunter]] at the [[Salk Institute for Biological Studies|Salk Institute]] in [[La Jolla]], California<ref name=zoo>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150515223837/http://www.zoo.cam.ac.uk/directory/jonathon-pines|archive-date=2015-05-15|url=http://www.zoo.cam.ac.uk/directory/jonathon-pines|title=Dr Jonathon Pines: Department of Zoology|publisher=University of Cambridge|location=Cambridge}}</ref><ref name=PinesHunter1990>{{cite journal|last1=Pines|first1=Jonathon|last2=Hunter|first2=Tony|title=Human cyclin A is adenovirus E1A-associated protein p60 and behaves differently from cyclin B|journal=Nature|volume=346|issue=6286|year=1990|pages=760–763|doi=10.1038/346760a0|pmid=2143810|bibcode=1990Natur.346..760P|s2cid=4333058}}</ref><ref name=HunterPines1991>{{cite journal|last1=Hunter|first1=Tony|last2=Pines|first2=Jonathon|title=Cyclins and cancer|journal=Cell|volume=66|issue=6|year=1991|pages=1071–1074|doi=10.1016/0092-8674(91)90028-W|pmid=1833062|s2cid=29568380}}</ref><ref name=HunterPines1994>{{cite journal|last1=Hunter|first1=Tony|last2=Pines|first2=Jonathon|title=Cyclins and cancer II: Cyclin D and CDK inhibitors come of age|journal=Cell|volume=79|issue=4|year=1994|pages=573–582|doi=10.1016/0092-8674(94)90543-6|pmid=7954824|s2cid=24867886}}</ref> before moving to the [[Gurdon Institute]] at the [[University of Cambridge]] then the [[Institute of Cancer Research]] in 2015.<ref name=gurdon/>

Pines research investigates cyclin, the [[cell cycle]] and [[mitosis]].<ref name=googlescholar/> He pioneered the use of [[fluorescent tag]]s to analyse the dynamic behaviour and stability of these regulators in living cells.<ref name=frs/>

Pines discoveries have revealed that mitotic regulators are targeted to specific substructures at specific times, and that mitosis is exquisitely coordinated by the destruction of key regulators at different times in cell division. Pines work has provided insights into how chromosome behaviour in mitosis controls both the time and the rate at which essential mitotic regulators are destroyed, and these discoveries have wider implications for how cancers develop.<ref name=frs/>

Since 2020, Pines has been [[Editor-in-Chief]] of the [[Royal Society]] journal ''[[Open Biology]].''

===Awards and honours===
Pines was elected a member of the [[European Molecular Biology Organisation|European Molecular Biology Organisation (EMBO)]] in 2001<ref name=embo>{{cite web|url=http://people.embo.org/profile/jonathon-pines|title=EMBO member: Jonathon Pines|publisher=EMBO|location=Heidelberg}}</ref> and a [[Academy of Medical Sciences, United Kingdom|Fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences (FMedSci)]] in 2005. His citation on election reads:

{{Quote|He has made key discoveries in the cell cycle field, many of which have opened up new avenues of research. He cloned the original 'cyclin' as a PhD student with [[Tim Hunt]] and demonstrated that it had mitosis-promoting activity. This discovery was essential to the subsequent cloning of ''[[Xenopus]]'' cyclins and kept the Hunt lab at the forefront of cyclin research. Subsequently he cloned and characterised the first human cyclins with [[Anthony R. Hunter|Tony Hunter]]. This was crucial to recognising that cyclins are conserved critical regulators of cell division. He provided the first evidence that there is a family of [[cyclin-dependent kinase]]s by identifying the second Cdk, [[Cyclin-dependent kinase 2|Cdk2]], and identified the first link between cyclins and [[oncoprotein]]s by showing that [[cyclin A]] bound to [[Adenovirus early region 1A|adenovirus E1A]], thus linking cyclins to the [[E2F]]/[[Retinoblastoma]] pathway. These discoveries sparked intensive efforts by many laboratories. In leading his own group he has shown the importance of analysing both the spatial and temporal control of the cell cycle, pioneering fluorescence [[time-lapse microscopy]] to study the cell cycle. After discovering that mitotic cyclins localise to different sub-cellular compartments he showed how they dynamically specify their localisation. Recently, he discovered that the mitotic kinase, [[cyclin B1]]-[[Cyclin-dependent kinase 1|Cdk1]] is activated on [[centrosome]]s, and thereby prompted considerable interest in the role of the centrosome in initiating mitosis. He has developed a novel live-cell assay for [[proteolysis]] and uncovered new mechanisms by which cells control mitosis. His analyses have shown how [[ubiquitin]]-mediated proteolysis coordinates chromosome congression with [[cytokinesis]] and [[mitotic exit]] by degrading specific proteins at specific times.<ref name=fmedsci/>}}

Pines was elected a [[List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 2016|Fellow of the Royal Society (FRS) in 2016]].<ref name=frs>{{cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/ramanujan-hegde-12876/ |title=Dr Jonathon Pines FRS |publisher=[[Royal Society]] |archive-date=2016-04-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160429121634/https://royalsociety.org/people/jonathon-pines-12890/ |location=London |author=Anon |year=2016 }} One or more of the preceding sentences incorporates text from the royalsociety.org website where: {{quote|"All text published under the heading 'Biography' on Fellow profile pages is available under [[Creative Commons license|Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License]]." --{{cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies/ |title=Royal Society Terms, conditions and policies |access-date=2016-03-09 |url-status=bot: unknown |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150925220834/https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies/ |archive-date=2015-09-25 }}}}</ref><ref>{{YouTube|id=z26mGqpSwAI|title=Professor Jonathon Pines on his election to the Royal Society}} Institute of Cancer Research, London</ref><ref>{{YouTube|id=6Z0fHo3cHbA|title=Professor Jonathon Pines elected as a Fellow of the Royal Society}} Institute of Cancer Research, London</ref>
